# Buddy mobile app control

Control the user's Android phone through the `mcp__buddy__*` tools. Use for any task phrased as "open app X", "tap Y", "check what's on screen", "watch/close the ad", "how long until Z".

## Procedure

0. **Pre-flight: check root readiness.** Call `mcp__buddy__root_status` before any screenshot/gesture. If it reports `KernelSU: NOT GRANTED`, stop and have the user authorize Buddy/root helper in KernelSU → Superuser, then re-check. `open_app` still succeeds without root, so a successful app open is not proof that gestures will work.
1. **Find the app.** `mcp__buddy__list_apps` returns installed apps with package names. Match the user's name to the label.
2. **Open it.** `mcp__buddy__open_app` with `app="<label>"`. Wait for load with `mcp__buddy__wait` (ms).
3. **Read native UI.** `mcp__buddy__read_screen` returns a numbered element list with ids and `@x,y` centers. Use element ids for native apps (dialogs, settings, browsers).
4. **Read graphics UI (games, canvas, video).** `read_screen` returns only a generic `Game view` node with no children — this does NOT mean the screen is empty. Take `mcp__buddy__screenshot` and analyze it with native image input: send the image to the model directly as an image content block via the Nous API (`references/vision-api.md`) so it sees shapes, colors, and layout, not just text. Reserve `vision_analyze` for a quick single-value read.
5. **Convert coordinates.** The screenshot result states its own size and the screen size plus a multiplier (e.g. 720x1600 image on 1080x2400 screen → multiply image coords by 1.5). Always convert image coords to screen coords before tapping. Tapping raw image coords misses.
6. **Tap.** `mcp__buddy__tap` with `x`,`y` (screen coords) or an element `id` from `read_screen`. For a popup that says "tap to close", tap its center.
7. **System keys.** `mcp__buddy__press` with `button` = `back` | `home` | `recents` | `notifications` | `quick_settings`.

## Pitfalls

- **Do not trust `read_screen` for games.** A "Game view" with no elements is the normal result for canvas/graphics rendering; the UI exists but is not in the accessibility tree. Fall back to screenshot + vision immediately instead of reporting "nothing is there" or guessing taps.
- **Check root readiness before any gesture or capture.** `screenshot`/`read_screen`/`swipe`/`tap`/`scroll` all need KernelSU root. Call `root_status` first. `open_app` still succeeds without root, so a successful open is not evidence that gestures work. Two distinct failures, and only one is fixed by a Superuser grant:
  - `KernelSU/su could not be started` (screenshot/read_screen) or `Swipe not performed: UNAVAILABLE` (swipe/tap/scroll) = Buddy could not exec `/system/bin/su` at all. A KernelSU grant does not help — KernelSU is never reached. Audit the su binary/manager module per `references/root-diagnosis.md`; do not just ask the user to re-grant.
  - `Root command failed: <message>` = su ran and KernelSU refused; this is the case a KernelSU → Superuser grant for `app.buddy.assistant` fixes.
  Trust `root_status` over the user's "I already granted it" — re-check after they grant, because a pending, denied, or mistargeted grant leaves the status unchanged.
- **Confirm the target app is foregrounded before reading.** The phone may still show a terminal, launcher, or the last-opened app; a screenshot of the wrong app yields confident-but-wrong readings. Open the app, wait for it to load, then screenshot. Two things pull a game out of the foreground mid-task: (a) running `terminal` commands — they execute in the on-phone PRoot/Termux environment and bring Termux forward, so keep the open → screenshot → act flow free of terminal calls and re-open the app before each read; (b) the user switching to the Linux/Termux view to watch the agent work — if a screenshot shows a terminal, re-open the game instead of concluding a tap missed.
- **A fresh open can still be on the loading screen.** Right after `open_app`, the capture may show the game's loading art/TIP screen instead of the playfield. Wait a few seconds and re-screenshot; do not analyze the loading screen or report its text as game state.
- **Always convert image coordinates to screen coordinates.** The screenshot is scaled down from the real screen; raw image coordinates land in the wrong place.
- **The on-screen keyboard covers lower controls.** Swipe up on the scroll container to reveal buttons hidden behind it; do not press `back` to dismiss the keyboard — on form screens back can exit the whole view and discard entered state.
- **Swipe tool requires all four arguments.** `mcp__buddy__swipe` silently fails with JSON validation errors if any of x1, y1, x2, y2 is missing. Always supply all four coordinates explicitly in the call.
- **MIUI settings toggles are often missing from `read_screen`.** When a settings page exposes no switch element, do not conclude the toggle is absent — screenshot, crop the row with PIL, locate the switch with the vision API, and tap by converted coordinates. See `references/macrodroid-setup.md`.
- **`read_screen` can render an EditText's text with single quotes even when the real content uses double quotes** (accessibility normalization). Before concluding that pasted JSON was mangled, confirm with a screenshot + vision read.
- **Clipboard tools ask the user for approval on every call** (`clipboard_read`, `clipboard_write`). To paste into a field: `clipboard_write` the text, tap the field, `long_press` it, then tap "Paste" in the popup.
- **`mcp__buddy__wait` caps at ~10000 ms per call.** For longer waits, call it repeatedly; do not assume one call covers a 30 s ad.
- **Verify a tap landed.** After tapping, re-screenshot and check visually — the accessibility read often still reports the unchanged "Game view" even when the tap worked.
- **Rewarded ads:** tapping a boost/ad button opens a full-screen ad. Wait it out, then look for a close (X) button via screenshot+vision (it may be a small circular X near the bottom). The close control can sit next to a Google Play / Download link — confirm with vision before tapping so you do not open the store. See `references/rewarded-ad-flow.md`.
- **After an ad closes, the app may be backgrounded or redirected** (e.g. Play Store opened over it). Re-open the app with `open_app` and confirm the reward via screenshot rather than assuming the game is still foregrounded.
- **Ad reward confirmation:** compare the timer/value before and after the ad (e.g. boost duration increased) to confirm the reward was granted.
- **Vision can be rate-limited.** If `vision_analyze` returns 429, do not wait idly or guess coordinates — fall back to MacroDroid's ML Kit OCR (best for game/canvas text; see `references/macrodroid-setup.md`) or tesseract with preprocessing (see `references/ocr-fallback.md`), and retry vision only after the stated `retry_after`. Pixel-art game fonts often defeat tesseract on small countdown pills, so treat OCR values as provisional and prefer a fresh vision read for any number you are about to act on.
- **For scripted or cron reads, call the Nous vision API directly.** `vision_analyze` can 404 inside a cron session and `execute_code` is blocked there; a script can call the Nous API with the free `meituan/longcat-2.5:free` model to read the same screenshot. See `references/vision-api.md`.
- **Do not burn turns on manual polling loops.** When the task is recurring (read a timer, act when a machine finishes, keep a boost topped up), prove the reading works once, then hand the repetition to a scheduled job (`cronjob_manage`) with a self-contained prompt. The user prefers a set-and-forget schedule over the agent re-checking turn after turn. See `references/scheduled-automation.md`.
- **Check the lock state before planning a wake.** `open_app` wakes the display and foregrounds the target in one step, so treat it as the way to "wake the screen" for an automation run. It only works on an unlocked phone: with a secure lock set, every buddy action fails with "Phone is locked" until the user unlocks, and a "nothing happened" report right after the screen went off is usually the lock, not a missed tap. The fix is a user setting, not a workaround — set the screen lock to None (Settings > Security > Screen lock > None) so the phone stays unlocked with the screen off, or keep it unlocked. Plan wake/unlock around that setting; do not budget turns for a root keyevent path, because the agent's shell runs in the untrusted_app SELinux context and cannot inject input events. See `references/screen-wake.md` for the Macrodroid and stay-awake alternatives. For generating MacroDroid macros from a description (AI Macro Builder) and MacroDroid↔Hermes integration options, see `references/macrodroid-ai-macro-builder.md`; for MacroDroid permissions, the MIUI toggle workaround, and its ML Kit OCR for reading game screens, see `references/macrodroid-setup.md`.

## User preference

The user expects elements to be identified from screenshots/vision, not guessed. When a screen is graphics-rendered, go straight to screenshot + vision and report concrete on-screen text, numbers, and timers rather than asking the user to describe the UI.

The user prefers native image input over the `vision_analyze` auxiliary tool: send the image directly to the model (Nous API, `meituan/longcat-2.5:free`) so it sees the actual pixels — shapes, colors, relative positions — rather than a text summary from a separate vision pass. For visual inventory tasks, present the result as a table and separate clearly-visible items from estimates and unrecognizable ones; the user wants uncertainty made explicit, not smoothed over.

The user does not want the agent to grind through manual retry/poll loops in the chat. Verify the measurement once, then put the repetition into a scheduled job. Reports should be short and concrete (timers read, action taken, final state), not a narration of each attempt.

When the user says to stop or remove a schedule "for now" (e.g. "hilangkan dulu", "matikan dulu"), pause it — they mean temporarily, and the prompt and schedule should survive for a later resume. Remove only when they ask for it permanently.

The user pre-approves device settings and permission grants — make settings changes and grant permission dialogs without asking for confirmation first.

For scripted/headless device work, the Buddy MCP server can be called directly over HTTP — see `references/mcp-http-api.md`.

When the user says "stop" or "just give me" the result, stop calling tools immediately and report what the current capture already shows — no further background jobs, re-runs, or verification passes.

Chrome/Chromium via CDP, no Playwright or Puppeteer dependency.
Accessibility-tree snapshots with compact `@eN` refs let agents interact with pages in ~200-400 tokens instead of parsing raw HTML.
Most normal web tasks (navigate, read, click, fill, extract, screenshot) are covered here.

agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. `snapshot` returns the page as compact text with a ref such as `@e1` for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. ## Install ```bash npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) ``` - **Homebrew:** `brew install agent-browser`, then `agent-browser install`. - **Linux:** `agent-browser install --with-deps` also installs the browser's system libraries. - **No install:** `npx agent-browser open example.com`. Project installs, building from source, `upgrade`, and `doctor` are covered in [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/installation). ## Quick start ```bash agent-browser open example.com agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-browser get url # check the result agent-browser close ``` The snapshot for `example.com`: ``` - link "Learn more" [ref=e1] ``` - Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again. - CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example `agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit"`. See [Selectors](https://agent-browser.dev/selectors). - A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry. The full walkthrough is in the [quick start](https://agent-browser.dev/quick-start). ## How it works The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each `--session` gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when [session persistence](https://agent-browser.dev/sessions) is configured. Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with `--cdp` or `--auto-connect` ([CDP mode](https://agent-browser.dev/cdp-mode)), select the [Lightpanda](https://agent-browser.dev/engines/lightpanda) or [Obscura](https://agent-browser.dev/engines/obscura) engine with `--engine`, drive Mobile Safari in the [iOS Simulator](https://agent-browser.dev/ios), or use a cloud browser provider such as [Browserbase](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/browserbase), [Browserless](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/browserless), [Browser Use](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/browser-use), [Kernel](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/kernel), or [AgentCore](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/agentcore). ## For AI agents The CLI ships skills that match its version: ```bash agent-browser skills get core # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows agent-browser skills get core --ref commands # one reference, such as the full command list agent-browser skills get core --full # adds the full command reference and templates agent-browser skills list # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more ``` Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-browser): ```bash npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser ``` The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load `agent-browser skills get core`, so its instructions always match the installed CLI. # agent-browser

Fast browser automation CLI for AI agents. Chrome/Chromium via CDP with accessibility-tree snapshots and compact `@eN` element refs.

Install: `npm i -g agent-browser && agent-browser install`

## Start here

This file is a discovery stub, not the usage guide. Before running any `agent-browser` command, load the actual workflow content from the CLI:

```bash
agent-browser skills get core             # start here: the loop, waits, common tasks, troubleshooting
```

The core guide ends with a table of references to load for detailed commands and flags. Use `agent-browser skills get core --full` only when you need every reference at once; it is several times larger.

The CLI serves skill content that matches the installed version. This stub cannot change between releases, which is why it only points at `skills get core`.

## Specialized skills

Load a specialized skill when the task falls outside browser web pages:

```bash
agent-browser skills get electron          # Electron desktop apps (VS Code, Slack, Discord, Figma, ...)
agent-browser skills get slack             # Slack workspace automation
agent-browser skills get dogfood           # Exploratory testing / QA / bug hunts
agent-browser skills get derive-client     # Record a HAR, derive a standalone API client for a site
agent-browser skills get webmcp-gen        # Build and validate WebMCP tools for a page
agent-browser skills get modern-web-guidance  # Apply Modern Web Guidance, then verify the page

agent-browser skills get agentcore         # AWS Bedrock AgentCore cloud browsers
```

Run `agent-browser skills list` to see everything available on the installed version.

- Fast native Rust CLI, not a Node.js wrapper
- Works with any AI agent (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Continue, Windsurf, etc.)
- Chrome/Chromium via CDP with no Playwright or Puppeteer dependency
- Accessibility-tree snapshots with element refs for reliable interaction
- Sessions, authentication vault, state persistence, video recording
- Specialized skills for Electron apps, Slack, exploratory testing, cloud providers

# Hermes Agent

Hermes Agent is an open-source AI agent framework by Nous Research that runs in your terminal, a native desktop app, messaging platforms, and IDEs. It's in the same category as Claude Code (Anthropic), Codex (OpenAI), and OpenClaw — autonomous coding and task-execution agents that use tool calling to interact with your system. Hermes works with any LLM provider (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, xAI, local models, and 20+ others) and runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, and WSL.

What makes Hermes different:

- **Self-improving through skills** — Hermes learns from experience by saving reusable procedures as skills that load into future sessions.
- **Persistent memory across sessions** — remembers who you are, your preferences, environment details, and lessons learned. Pluggable memory backends.
- **Multi-platform gateway** — the same agent runs on Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, iMessage, Signal, Matrix, Teams, Email, and a dozen more platforms with full tool access, not just chat.
- **Many surfaces** — the same agent core drives the CLI, the Ink TUI, a native Electron desktop app, a web dashboard, and an ACP server for IDEs (VS Code / Zed / JetBrains).
- **Provider-agnostic** — swap models and providers mid-workflow; credential pools rotate across multiple API keys automatically.
- **Profiles** — run multiple independent Hermes instances with isolated configs, sessions, skills, and memory.
- **Extensible & themeable** — plugins, MCP servers, custom tools, webhook triggers, cron scheduling, skins that theme every surface, desktop UI plugins, TUI widgets, and pet mascots.

**This skill is a hub.** The body covers identity, quick start, spawning/orchestration, and hard invariants. Everything else lives in reference files — **load the matching reference (below) before answering**; do not answer detail questions from the body alone.

**Docs:** https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/

This skill is a concise operating guide, not the complete source of truth for every Hermes feature. If a Hermes feature, command, or setting is not mentioned here or in a reference, do not treat that absence as evidence that it does not exist. Check the live repository and official docs before giving a negative answer.

- **Every shipped feature, one line each: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/llms.txt.** Start here for any "can Hermes do X?" or "how do I do X?" — it indexes the entire documentation set with a link to the page that answers. It is generated from the docs tree on every build, so it is never behind the product. Fetch it with `web_extract`, or `curl -s https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/llms.txt` when web tools are off. The whole documentation set in one file is at `/docs/llms-full.txt`.
- CLI commands: `hermes --help`, `hermes <command> --help`, and `hermes_cli/main.py`
- Source tree: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent

Never answer "Hermes can't do that" from memory. Hermes ships far more than this skill body describes, and the index exists so a negative answer is always checkable.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Install (shell installer — bootstraps PM, Python, dependencies, and the launcher)
curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash

# Interactive chat (default surface; set display.interface: tui to launch the Ink TUI instead)
hermes

# Single query
hermes chat -q "What is the capital of France?"

# Setup wizard  /  pick model+provider  /  health check
hermes setup
hermes model
hermes doctor

# Other surfaces
hermes desktop                 # launch the native desktop app (alias: hermes gui)
hermes dashboard               # web admin panel + embedded chat
hermes proxy                   # OpenAI-compatible local proxy backed by your OAuth provider
```

## Key Paths

```
~/.hermes/config.yaml       Main configuration (settings — never secrets)
~/.hermes/.env              API keys and secrets ONLY (under $HERMES_HOME if set)
$HERMES_HOME/skills/        Installed skills
~/.hermes/skins/            Custom themes (see references/themes.md)
~/.hermes/desktop-plugins/  Desktop app UI plugins (see references/desktop-plugins.md)
~/.hermes/tui-widgets/      TUI widget apps (see references/tui-widgets.md)
~/.hermes/pets/             Installed pet mascots (see references/petdex.md)
~/.hermes/state.db          Canonical session store (SQLite + FTS5)
~/.hermes/sessions/         Gateway routing index, request dumps, *.jsonl transcripts
~/.hermes/logs/             Gateway and error logs
~/.hermes/auth.json         OAuth tokens and credential pools
~/.hermes/hermes-agent/     Source code (if git-installed)
```

Profiles use `~/.hermes/profiles/<name>/` with the same layout. When a profile is active, resolve the real home from `$HERMES_HOME` — never hardcode `~/.hermes`.

## Spawning Additional Hermes Instances

Run additional Hermes processes as fully independent subprocesses — separate sessions, tools, and environments.

### When to Use This vs delegate_task

| | `delegate_task` | Spawning `hermes` process |
|-|-----------------|--------------------------|
| Isolation | Separate conversation, shared process | Fully independent process |
| Duration | Minutes (bounded by parent loop) | Hours/days |
| Tool access | Subset of parent's tools | Full tool access |
| Interactive | No | Yes (PTY mode) |
| Use case | Quick parallel subtasks | Long autonomous missions |

### One-Shot Mode

`hermes -z` / `--oneshot` is the script/pipe form: one prompt, final response text only, no banner, spinner, tool previews, or session_id line. Approvals are auto-bypassed. Pair it with `--usage-file PATH` (see `references/cli-reference.md`).

```
terminal(command="hermes -z 'Research GRPO papers and write summary to ~/research/grpo.md' --usage-file /tmp/run-usage.json", timeout=300)

# Background for long tasks:
terminal(command="hermes -z 'Set up CI/CD for ~/myapp'", background=true)

# Same prompt, interactive chat surface:
terminal(command="hermes chat -q 'Research GRPO papers and write summary to ~/research/grpo.md'", timeout=300)
```

Argument order matters: put the prompt IMMEDIATELY after `-z`, before any other
flag — `hermes -z "PROMPT" -t terminal --usage-file PATH`. `hermes -z -t terminal
...` parses the flag as the prompt's value and exits 2 with `argument -z/--oneshot:
expected one argument`; argparse never consumes a `-`-prefixed token as an option's
value. To prove a flag combination without spending a model call, import the parser
and call `parse_args` on a fabricated `sys.argv` (refuses with `SystemExit: 2`).

### Interactive PTY Mode (via tmux)

Hermes uses prompt_toolkit, which requires a real terminal. Use tmux for interactive spawning. `tmux send-keys -t agent1 'text' Enter` in one call submits: Hermes treats a lone Enter that ends a fast burst of input as a submit once input has stayed quiet for a quarter second, while the Enters inside a multi-line paste stay newlines. The recipes below send `Enter` as its own call after a short pause, which submits at once and does not depend on that timing. Both recipes wait for the `❯` input prompt (the default skin's symbol; use your skin's prompt symbol if you changed it) instead of a fixed sleep: a first start can take far longer than a few seconds, and input sent before the prompt is lost.

```
# Start
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s agent1 -x 120 -y 40 'hermes'", timeout=10)

# Wait for the input prompt (❯), then send a message
terminal(command="for i in $(seq 90); do tmux capture-pane -t agent1 -p | grep -q '❯' && break; sleep 1; done; tmux capture-pane -t agent1 -p | grep -q '❯' && tmux send-keys -t agent1 'Build a FastAPI auth service' && sleep 0.5 && tmux send-keys -t agent1 Enter", timeout=100)

# Read output
terminal(command="sleep 20 && tmux capture-pane -t agent1 -p", timeout=5)

# Send follow-up
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t agent1 'Add rate limiting middleware' && sleep 0.5 && tmux send-keys -t agent1 Enter", timeout=5)

# Exit
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t agent1 '/exit' && sleep 0.5 && tmux send-keys -t agent1 Enter && sleep 2 && tmux kill-session -t agent1", timeout=10)
```

**No tmux** (`command -v tmux` prints nothing, e.g. an older Hermes Docker image): run Hermes as a PTY background process and drive it with `process_manage`. Stdin only exists with `pty=true`. `submit` sends the text plus the Enter key a keyboard sends, and Hermes submits it the same way as a one-call tmux `send-keys`. The recipe below instead `write`s the text, pauses, and `write`s the Enter (`"\r"`) on its own, which does not depend on burst timing. Wait for the input prompt before the first write: during startup Hermes queries the terminal's colours and then flushes its input, so text written before the prompt appears is silently dropped.

```
terminal(command="hermes", background=true, pty=true)   # returns session_id
process_manage(action="log", session_id="<id>", limit=20)   # repeat, with terminal(command="sleep 1") between, until the ❯ prompt line shows
process_manage(action="write", session_id="<id>", data="Build a FastAPI auth service")
terminal(command="sleep 0.5")
process_manage(action="write", session_id="<id>", data="\r")
process_manage(action="log", session_id="<id>", limit=40)   # read the screen
process_manage(action="write", session_id="<id>", data="/exit")
terminal(command="sleep 0.5")
process_manage(action="write", session_id="<id>", data="\r")
```

### Multi-Agent Coordination

```
# Agent A: backend
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s backend -x 120 -y 40 'hermes -w'", timeout=10)
terminal(command="for i in $(seq 90); do tmux capture-pane -t backend -p | grep -q '❯' && break; sleep 1; done; tmux capture-pane -t backend -p | grep -q '❯' && tmux send-keys -t backend 'Build REST API for user management' && sleep 0.5 && tmux send-keys -t backend Enter", timeout=100)

# Agent B: frontend
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s frontend -x 120 -y 40 'hermes -w'", timeout=10)
terminal(command="for i in $(seq 90); do tmux capture-pane -t frontend -p | grep -q '❯' && break; sleep 1; done; tmux capture-pane -t frontend -p | grep -q '❯' && tmux send-keys -t frontend 'Build React dashboard for user management' && sleep 0.5 && tmux send-keys -t frontend Enter", timeout=100)

# Check progress, relay context between them
terminal(command="tmux capture-pane -t backend -p | tail -30", timeout=5)
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t frontend 'Here is the API schema from the backend agent: ...' && sleep 0.5 && tmux send-keys -t frontend Enter", timeout=5)
```

### Session Resume

```
# Resume most recent session
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s resumed 'hermes --continue'", timeout=10)

# Resume specific session
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s resumed 'hermes --resume 20260225_143052_a1b2c3'", timeout=10)
```

### Tips

- **Prefer `delegate_task` for quick subtasks** — less overhead than spawning a full process
- **Use `-w` (worktree mode)** when spawning agents that edit code — prevents git conflicts
- **Set timeouts** for one-shot mode — complex tasks can take 5-10 minutes
- **Use `hermes chat -q` for fire-and-forget** — no PTY needed
- **Prefer tmux for interactive sessions when it is installed** — `capture-pane` reads the rendered screen; the PTY-background fallback only has the raw output log
- **For scheduled tasks**, use the `cronjob` tool instead of spawning — handles delivery and retry
- **"delegate_task is capped at N" reports** — see `references/delegate-task-concurrency-diagnosis.md`. Three real cap paths in Hermes; if none fired, the model is self-limiting and rationalising it as "the runtime caps."
- **"Can $external_app use my Nous Portal subscription / OAuth?"** — see `references/portal-auth-for-third-party-apps.md`. Walk the user through three layers (plugin-vs-app, what Portal actually exposes, local-broker-proxy option).

## Surfaces (quick orientation)

- **Desktop app** (`hermes desktop` / `hermes gui`) — native Electron app for macOS/Linux/Windows: streaming chat, session list, Cmd+K palette, drag-and-drop files, native notifications, per-profile remote-gateway login. Extend it with UI plugins — `references/desktop-plugins.md`.
- **Web dashboard** (`hermes dashboard`) — full admin panel: messaging channels, MCP catalog, webhooks, memory, profile builder, plus an embedded `hermes --tui` chat. Secured behind an OAuth/token gate.
- **Ink TUI** (`hermes --tui` or `display.interface: tui`) — terminal UI with docked widget apps — `references/tui-widgets.md`.
- **OpenAI-compatible proxy** (`hermes proxy`) — a local OpenAI API backed by whichever OAuth provider you're signed into. Point Codex CLI, Aider, Cline, or any script at it — no API key.

## Read-only audit reports

When the user asks for a read-only audit ("AUDIT READ-ONLY", "periksa kode saja",
"jangan mengubah apa pun"), the deliverable is evidence, not a plan or a fix:

- Honour the boundary literally — no writes to files, `config.yaml`, skills, or
  source. Never "verify" by running a mutating command (`hermes config set`,
  `/reset`, a screenshot the user ruled out); read the code and call pure
  functions instead.
- Every claim carries `path:line` plus the quoted code. An uncited claim is a
  guess — label it as one, and keep proven fact and inference in separate
  sentences.
- Follow the mandated report shape exactly: word cap, conclusion labels
  (A/B/C…), section order. Do not add a todo list or a test plan the user
  excluded.
- Batch reads and greps per file rather than one call per lookup, and cite the
  line numbers actually seen.

## Hard Invariants (never violate, regardless of what you loaded)

- **Never break prompt caching** — don't change past context, toolsets, or the system prompt mid-conversation. The only exception is context compression.
- **Message role alternation** — never two assistant or two user messages in a row; only `tool` results can repeat.
- **Secrets in `.env`, settings in `config.yaml`** — never tell a user to put a non-credential setting in `.env`.
- **Profile-safe paths** — `get_hermes_home()` in code, `$HERMES_HOME` when resolving paths in a session.
- **Never hand-edit `config.yaml` for the user** — use `hermes config set KEY VAL`; a stray indent can corrupt the file and break the live gateway.

Four systems run alongside the main conversation loop. Quick reference
here; full developer notes live in `AGENTS.md`, user-facing docs under
`website/docs/user-guide/features/`.

### Delegation (`delegate_task`)

Spawn a subagent with an isolated context + terminal session.

- **Single:** `delegate_task(goal, context)`.
- **Batch:** `delegate_task(tasks=[{goal, ...}, ...])` runs children in
  parallel, capped by `delegation.max_concurrent_children` (default 3).
- **Background:** `delegate_task(background=true)` returns a handle
  immediately and keeps the parent loop going; the child's result
  re-enters the conversation as a new turn when it finishes.
- **Roles:** `leaf` (default; cannot re-delegate) vs `orchestrator`
  (can spawn its own workers, bounded by `delegation.max_spawn_depth`).
- **Not durable.** A backgrounded child is still process-local — if the
  parent process exits, the child is lost. For work that must outlive
  the process, use `cronjob` or
  `terminal(background=True, notify_on_complete=True)`.

Config: `delegation.*` in `config.yaml`.

### Cron (scheduled jobs)

Durable scheduler — `cron/jobs.py` + `cron/scheduler.py`. Drive it via
the `cronjob` tool, the `hermes cron` CLI (`list`, `add`, `edit`,
`pause`, `resume`, `run`, `remove`), or the `/cron` slash command.

- **Schedules:** duration (`"30m"`, `"2h"`), "every" phrase
  (`"every monday 9am"`), 5-field cron (`"0 9 * * *"`), or ISO timestamp.
- **Per-job knobs:** `skills`, `model`/`provider` override, `script`
  (pre-run data collection; `no_agent=True` makes the script the whole
  job), `context_from` (chain job A's output into job B), `workdir`
  (run in a specific dir with its `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` loaded),
  multi-platform delivery.
- **Invariants:** 3-minute hard interrupt per run, `.tick.lock` file
  prevents duplicate ticks across processes, cron sessions pass
  `skip_memory=True` by default, and cron deliveries are framed with a
  header/footer instead of being mirrored into the target gateway
  session (keeps role alternation intact).

- **Stopping a job:** `pause` for a temporary stop — it keeps the prompt,
  schedule, and run history so `resume` brings the job back intact; use
  `remove` only when the user means it permanently. When a job stops
  delivering or the user says it is misbehaving, run `list` first and read
  `last_status` / `last_error` (e.g. `interrupted` = the 3-minute hard
  interrupt fired) before changing or re-creating anything.

User docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/cron

### Curator (skill lifecycle)

Background maintenance for agent-created skills. Tracks usage, marks
idle skills stale, archives stale ones, keeps a pre-run tar.gz backup
so nothing is lost.

- **CLI:** `hermes curator <verb>` — `status`, `usage`, `run`, `pause`,
  `resume`, `pin`, `unpin`, `archive`, `restore`, `list-archived`, `prune`,
  `backup`, `rollback`.
- **Slash:** `/curator <subcommand>` mirrors the CLI.
- **Scope:** only touches skills with `created_by: "agent"` provenance.
  Bundled + hub-installed skills are off-limits. **Never deletes** —
  max destructive action is archive. Pinned skills are exempt from
  every auto-transition and every LLM review pass.
- **Cost:** the deterministic inactivity/prune sweep runs for free. The
  aux-model "consolidate overlapping skills into umbrellas" pass is
  **off by default** — opt in with `curator.consolidate: true` or
  `hermes curator run --consolidate`. Routine background curation costs
  zero tokens.
- **Telemetry:** sidecar at `~/.hermes/skills/.usage.json` holds
  per-skill `use_count`, `view_count`, `patch_count`,
  `last_activity_at`, `state`, `pinned`.
- **Proving a skill changed (forensics):** `~/.hermes/skills/.curator_ledger.jsonl`
  is append-only JSONL — one entry per `write_file`/`patch` with `actor`, `ts`,
  the file path, and `before`/`after` sha256. `~/.hermes/.curator_backups/blobs/`
  stores every version content-addressed by its sha256, so `diff <blobA> <blobB>`
  shows exactly what changed. Hash the live file first: if its sha256 equals a
  blob, that blob IS the current content, not the previous one. Report location,
  mtime, hash, and the last before→after pair — never restore or edit.

Config: `curator.*` (`enabled`, `interval_hours`, `min_idle_hours`,
`stale_after_days`, `archive_after_days`, `backup.*`).
User docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/curator

### Kanban (multi-agent work queue)

Durable SQLite board for multi-profile / multi-worker collaboration.
Users drive it via `hermes kanban <verb>`; dispatcher-spawned workers
see a focused `kanban_*` toolset gated by `HERMES_KANBAN_TASK`, and
orchestrator profiles can opt into the broader `kanban` toolset. Normal
sessions still have zero `kanban_*` schema footprint unless configured.

- **CLI verbs (common):** `init`, `create`, `list` (alias `ls`),
  `show`, `assign`, `link`, `unlink`, `comment`, `complete`, `block`,
  `unblock`, `archive`, `tail`. Less common: `watch`, `stats`, `runs`,
  `log`, `dispatch`, `daemon`, `gc`.
- **Worker/orchestrator toolset:** `kanban_show`, `kanban_complete`,
  `kanban_block`, `kanban_heartbeat`, `kanban_comment`, `kanban_create`,
  `kanban_link`; profiles that explicitly enable the `kanban` toolset
  outside a dispatcher-spawned task also get `kanban_list` and
  `kanban_unblock` for board routing.
- **Dispatcher** runs inside the gateway by default
  (`kanban.dispatch_in_gateway: true`) — reclaims stale claims,
  promotes ready tasks, atomically claims, spawns assigned profiles.
  Auto-blocks a task after `failure_limit` consecutive spawn failures
  (default 2; configurable via `kanban.failure_limit` or per-task
  `max_retries`).
- **Isolation:** board is the hard boundary (workers get
  `HERMES_KANBAN_BOARD` pinned in env); tenant is a soft namespace
  within a board for workspace-path + memory-key isolation.

Project-linked tasks (worktree + branch by default under a Project's primary folder, when it has one):
`references/projects-and-folders.md`.
User docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/kanban

# Managing Hermes Skills

Install, update, inspect, and remove skills — from a registry identifier, a
GitHub repo, or a direct SKILL.md URL.

## Install

```bash
hermes skills install <identifier> [--category DIR] [--name NAME] [--force] [-y]
```

`<identifier>` is either a registry identifier (`owner/repo/skill-name`) or a
direct HTTP(S) URL to the SKILL.md file itself. For a GitHub repo, resolve the
raw URL to the exact SKILL.md path — the repo root is not an identifier:

```
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<branch>/<path>/SKILL.md
```

Find the path in the repo tree
(`https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/git/trees/<branch>?recursive=1`)
or on the file page. `-y` skips the confirmation prompt (needed in
non-interactive contexts).

The installer prints a security-scan verdict and hash. Read a non-SAFE verdict
before retrying with `--force`, which bypasses the block.

## Name collisions — back up before --force

A skill with the same name already present (bundled, hub-installed, or a local
copy) makes the install refuse or replace it; `--force` is the intended way
past that, but it overwrites the live skill directory and takes any local edits
with it.

Before forcing an overwrite:

```bash
cp -a "$HERMES_HOME/skills/<name>" "$TMPDIR/<name>.bak.$(date +%s)"
```

Then `diff -u` the backup against the incoming file to see exactly what will be
lost. Curator's archive/rollback only covers skills with agent provenance, so a
hand-edited or URL-installed skill has no automatic recovery path.

Resolve paths with `$HERMES_HOME` when a profile is active — never hardcode
`~/.hermes`.

## Verify after install

Three checks, cheapest first:

1. `diff -q "$HERMES_HOME/skills/<name>/SKILL.md" /tmp/incoming.md` — the
   installed bytes equal the source you asked for.
2. `hermes skills list | grep <name>` — status `enabled`; a URL install shows
   `source: url` and `trust: community` until vetted.
3. `skill_view('<name>')` loads the NEW content — the proof the loader sees the
   replacement, not the previously cached copy.

## Stub skills depend on their CLI

Many upstream repos ship a SKILL.md that is deliberately a discovery stub: it
tells the agent to run `<cli> skills get <topic>`, and the real procedure text is
served by a companion CLI binary matching the installed version. Installing the
SKILL.md therefore does NOT make the skill usable.

Before calling the install done, check for the companion binary:

```bash
command -v <cli>
```

If it is absent, report the separate install step (e.g.
`npm i -g <pkg> && <cli> install`) and let the user decide — that step usually
fetches a browser/runtime and is too large to run silently. Never claim a skill
"works" when only the stub landed.

## Verbs worth knowing

- `hermes skills inspect <identifier>` — preview a candidate skill's
  frontmatter and description before installing it.
- `hermes skills list`, `list-modified`, `diff` — library state, local edits to
  bundled skills, and divergence from stock.
- `hermes skills check`, `update` — hub-tracked skills only; a URL or local
  install is not tracked, so refresh those deliberately.

{"success": true, "name": "hermes-agent", "file": "references/skills-management.md", "content": "# Managing Hermes Skills

Install, update, inspect, and remove skills — from a registry identifier, a
GitHub repo, or a direct SKILL.md URL.

## Install

```bash
hermes skills install <identifier> [--category DIR] [--name NAME] [--force] [-y]
```

`<identifier>` is either a registry identifier (`owner/repo/skill-name`) or a
direct HTTP(S) URL to the SKILL.md file itself. For a GitHub repo, resolve the
raw URL to the exact SKILL.md path — the repo root is not an identifier:

```
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<branch>/<path>/SKILL.md
```

Find the path in the repo tree
(`https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/git/trees/<branch>?recursive=1`)
or on the file page. `-y` skips the confirmation prompt (needed in
non-interactive contexts).

The installer prints a security-scan verdict and hash. Read a non-SAFE verdict
before retrying with `--force`, which bypasses the block.

## Name collisions — back up before --force

A skill with the same name already present (bundled, hub-installed, or a local
copy) makes the install refuse or replace it; `--force` is the intended way
past that, but it overwrites the live skill directory and takes any local edits
with it.

Before forcing an overwrite:

```bash
cp -a "$HERMES_HOME/skills/<name>" "$TMPDIR/<name>.bak.$(date +%s)"
```

Then `diff -u` the backup against the incoming file to see exactly what will be
lost. Curator's archive/rollback only covers skills with agent provenance, so a
hand-edited or URL-installed skill has no automatic recovery path.

Resolve paths with `$HERMES_HOME` when a profile is active — never hardcode
`~/.hermes`.

## Verify after install

Three checks, cheapest first:

1. `diff -q "$HERMES_HOME/skills/<name>/SKILL.md" /tmp/incoming.md` — the
   installed bytes equal the source you asked for.
2. `hermes skills list | grep <name>` — status `enabled`; a URL install shows
   `source: url` and `trust: community` until vetted.
3. `skill_view('<name>')` loads the NEW content — the proof the loader sees the
   replacement, not the previously cached copy.

## Stub skills depend on their CLI

Many upstream repos ship a SKILL.md that is deliberately a discovery stub: it
tells the agent to run `<cli> skills get <topic>`, and the real procedure text is
served by a companion CLI binary matching the installed version. Installing the
SKILL.md therefore does NOT make the skill usable.

Before calling the install done, check for the companion binary:

```bash
command -v <cli>
```

If it is absent, report the separate install step (e.g.
`npm i -g <pkg> && <cli> install`) and let the user decide — that step usually
fetches a browser/runtime and is too large to run silently. Never claim a skill
"works" when only the stub landed.

## Verbs worth knowing

- `hermes skills inspect <identifier>` — preview a candidate skill's
  frontmatter and description before installing it.
- `hermes skills list`, `list-modified`, `diff` — library state, local edits to
  bundled skills, and divergence from stock.
- `hermes skills check`, `update` — hub-tracked skills only; a URL or local
  install is not tracked, so refresh those deliberately.
- `hermes skills uninstall <name>`, `reset <name>` (clear user-modified
  tracking on a bundled skill), `config` (enable/disable individual skills).
- `hermes skills tap` — manage alternate skill sources/registries.
